title: Hands-on Exercise (Part 4)
text:
Computing the basic derived fields
Derive cumulative death rate and standard error of cumulative death rate.

df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death / Positive) %>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate*(1-rate)) / (Positive))) %>%
  filter(rate > 0)

The fit.mean is computed by using the code chunk below.

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1/df$rate.se^2)

title: Hands-on Exercise (Part 4)
section: Calculate lower and upper limits for 95% and 99.9% CI
text:
Calculate lower and upper limits for 95% and 99.9% CI

number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
dfCI <- data.frame(number.ll95, number.ul95, number.ll999, 
                   number.ul999, number.seq, fit.mean)

p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Positive, y = rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(label=`Sub-district`),

            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ll95), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40",

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 (Part 1)
section: Mapping the probabilities directly onto colour
text:
Mapping the probabilities directly onto colour
Figure below is plotted by mapping the probabilities calculated by using stat(ecdf) which represent the empirical cumulative density function for the distribution of English score.

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5-stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient", 
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 (Part 1)
text:
Ridgeline plots with quantile lines
By using geom_density_ridges_gradient(), we can colour the ridgeline plot by quantile, via the calculated stat(quantile) aesthetic as shown in the figure below.

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = 4,
    quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18









Instead of using number to define the quantiles, we can also specify quantiles by cut points such as 2.5% and 97.5% tails to colour the ridgeline plot as shown in the figure below.

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile))
           )) +
  stat_density_ridges(
    geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
    calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
    quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)
    ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#FF0000A0", "#A0A0A0A0", "#0000FFA0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +
  theme_ridges()

Picking joint bandwidth of 3.18

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
Code chunk below will be used to check, install and launch the following R packages:

ggiraph for making ‘ggplot’ graphics interactive.
plotly, R library for plotting interactive statistical graphs.
DT provides an R interface to the JavaScript library DataTables that create interactive table on html page.
tidyverse, a family of modern R packages specially designed to support data science, analysis and communication task including creating static statistical graphs.
patchwork for combining multiple ggplot2 graphs into one figure.


pacman::p_load(ggiraph, plotly, 
               patchwork, DT, tidyverse)

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
Tooltip effect with tooltip aesthetic
Below shows a typical code chunk to plot an interactive statistical graph by using ggiraph package.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE, 
    binwidth = 1, 
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, 
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6*0.618
)





By hovering the mouse pointer on an data point of interest, the student’s ID will be displayed.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
Displaying multiple information on tooltip
The content of the tooltip can be customised by including a list object as shown in the code chunk below.

exam_data$tooltip <- c(paste0(     
  "Name = ", exam_data$ID,         
  "\n Class = ", exam_data$CLASS)) 

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = exam_data$tooltip), 
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 8,
  height_svg = 8*0.618
)





By hovering the mouse pointer on an data point of interest, the student’s ID and Class will be displayed.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
Customising Tooltip style
Code chunk below uses opts_tooltip() of ggiraph to customize tooltip rendering by add css declarations.

tooltip_css <- "background-color:white; #<<
font-style:bold; color:black;" #<<

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(tooltip = ID),                   
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(    #<<
    opts_tooltip(    #<<
      css = tooltip_css)) #<<
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
Displaying statistics on tooltip
Code chunk below shows an advanced way to customise tooltip. In this example, a function is used to compute 90% confident interval of the mean. The derived statistics are then displayed in the tooltip.

tooltip <- function(y, ymax, accuracy = .01) {
  mean <- scales::number(y, accuracy = accuracy)
  sem <- scales::number(ymax - y, accuracy = accuracy)
  paste("Mean maths scores:", mean, "+/-", sem)
}

gg_point <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
                   aes(x = RACE),
) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS, 
                   tooltip = after_stat(  
                     tooltip(y, ymax))),  
    fun.data = "mean_se", 
    geom = GeomInteractiveCol,  
    fill = "light blue"
  ) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS),
    fun.data = mean_se,
    geom = "errorbar", width = 0.2, size = 0.2
  )

Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.

girafe(ggobj = gg_point,
       width_svg = 8,
       height_svg = 8*0.618)

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
Click effect with onclick
onclick argument of ggiraph provides hotlink interactivity on the web.
The code chunk below shown an example of onclick.

exam_data$onclick <- sprintf("window.open(\"%s%s\")",
"https://www.moe.gov.sg/schoolfinder?journey=Primary%20school",
as.character(exam_data$ID))

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +

    aes(onclick = onclick),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618)                                        





Interactivity: Web document link with a data object will be displayed on the web browser upon mouse click.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
Coordinated Multiple Views with ggiraph
In order to build a coordinated multiple views as shown in the exercise example, the following programming strategy will be used:

Appropriate interactive functions of ggiraph will be used to create the multiple views.
patchwork function of patchwork package will be used inside girafe function to create the interactive coordinated multiple views.


p1 <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = ID),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +  
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

p2 <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(data_id = ID),              
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)

girafe(code = print(p1 + p2), 
       width_svg = 6,
       height_svg = 3,
       options = list(
         opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),
         opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;")
         )
       ) 





Interactivity: When a data point of one of the dotplot is selected, the corresponding data point ID on the second data visualisation will be highlighted too.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
Coordinated Multiple Views with plotly
The creation of a coordinated linked plot by using plotly involves three steps:

highlight_key() of plotly package is used as shared data.
two scatterplots will be created by using ggplot2 functions.
lastly, subplot() of plotly package is used to place them next to each other side-by-side.


d <- highlight_key(exam_data)
p1 <- ggplot(data=d, 
            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))

p2 <- ggplot(data=d, 
            aes(x = MATHS,
                y = SCIENCE)) +
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))
subplot(ggplotly(p1),
        ggplotly(p2))

Interactive Data Table: DT package

A wrapper of the JavaScript Library DataTables

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
Linked brushing: crosstalk method
Code chunk below is used to implement the coordinated brushing.

d <- highlight_key(exam_data) 
p <- ggplot(d, 
            aes(ENGLISH, 
                MATHS)) + 
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))

gg <- highlight(ggplotly(p),        
                "plotly_selected")  

crosstalk::bscols(gg,               
                  DT::datatable(d), 
                  widths = 5)        

Setting the `off` event (i.e., 'plotly_deselect') to match the `on` event (i.e., 'plotly_selected'). You can change this default via the `highlight()` function.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
section: Building a static population bubble plot
text:
Building a static population bubble plot
In the code chunk below, the basic ggplot2 functions are used to create a static bubble plot.

ggplot(globalPop, aes(x = Old, y = Young, 
                      size = Population, 
                      colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, 
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(title = 'Year: {frame_time}', 
       x = '% Aged', 
       y = '% Young')

title: Hands-on Exercise 3
text:
Building the animated bubble plot
In the code chunk below,

transition_time() of gganimate is used to create transition through distinct states in time (i.e. Year).
ease_aes() is used to control easing of aesthetics. The default is linear. Other methods are: quadratic, cubic, quartic, quintic, sine, circular, exponential, elastic, back, and bounce.


ggplot(globalPop, aes(x = Old, y = Young, 
                      size = Population, 
                      colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, 
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(title = 'Year: {frame_time}', 
       x = '% Aged', 
       y = '% Young') +
  transition_time(Year) +       
  ease_aes('linear')

Warning in geom_point(aes(size = Population, frame = Year), alpha = 0.7, :
Ignoring unknown aesthetics: frame

ggplotly(gg)

Warning in p$x$data[firstFrame] <- p$x$frames[[1]]$data: number of items to
replace is not a multiple of replacement length






Even though show.legend = FALSE argument was used, the legend still appeared on the plot. To overcome this problem, theme(legend.position=‘none’) should be used as shown below.

gg <- ggplot(globalPop, 
       aes(x = Old, 
           y = Young, 
           size = Population, 
           colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = Population,
                 frame = Year),
             alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  labs(x = '% Aged', 
       y = '% Young') + 
  theme(legend.position='none')

Ignoring unknown aesthetics: frame

ggplotly(gg)

text:
pacman::p_load(ggstatsplot, tidyverse)





exam <- read_csv("data/Exam_data.csv")

dbl (3): ENGLISH, MATHS, SCIENCE

ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.





In the code chunk below, gghistostats() is used to to build an visual of one-sample test on English scores.

set.seed(1234)

gghistostats(
  data = exam,
  x = ENGLISH,
  type = "bayes",
  test.value = 60,
  xlab = "English scores"
)











In the code chunk below, ggbetweenstats() is used to build a visual for two-sample mean test of Maths scores by gender.

ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = GENDER, 
  y = MATHS,
  type = "np",
  messages = FALSE
)











In the code chunk below, ggbetweenstats() is used to build a visual for One-way ANOVA test on English score by race.

ggbetweenstats(
  data = exam,
  x = RACE, 
  y = ENGLISH,
  type = "p",
  mean.ci = TRUE, 
  pairwise.comparisons = TRUE, 
  pairwise.display = "s",
  p.adjust.method = "fdr",
  messages = FALSE
)











In the code chunk below, ggscatterstats() is used to build a visual for Significant Test of Correlation between Maths scores and English scores.

ggscatterstats(
  data = exam,
  x = MATHS,
  y = ENGLISH,
  marginal = FALSE,
  )











In the code chunk below, the Maths scores is binned into a 4-class variable by using cut().

exam1 <- exam %>% 
  mutate(MATHS_bins = 
           cut(MATHS, 
               breaks = c(0,60,75,85,100))
)

In this code chunk below ggbarstats() is used to build a visual for Significant Test of Association

ggbarstats(exam1, 
           x = MATHS_bins, 
           y = GENDER)

label <- function(txt) {

panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits=2, prefix="", cex.cor, ...) {
usr <- par("usr")
on.exit(par(usr))
par(usr = c(0, 1, 0, 1))
r <- abs(cor(x, y, use="complete.obs"))
txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits=digits)[1]
txt <- paste(prefix, txt, sep="")
if(missing(cex.cor)) cex.cor <- 0.8/strwidth(txt)
text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)
}

The colour scheme used is very copnfusing. This is because mapping = (min(values), mean(range(values)), max(values)). It is not wise to use diverging colour palette such as RdYlBu if the values are all positive or negative To overcome this problem, a single colour palette such as Blues should be used.

        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Exploring Ship Performance: Financial Insights via Visualisation
text:
The maritime industry is a key driver of global trade, directly impacting supply chains and economic growth. Efficient ship performance management is essential for maximizing profitability, reducing operational costs, and maintaining competitive advantages. By analyzing revenue generation, cost structures, and profitability across different ship types and routes, businesses can optimize fleet management strategies. Additionally, understanding operational efficiency and seasonal impacts allows companies to make data-driven decisions, improve resource allocation, and enhance overall financial performance, ultimately driving sustainable growth and profitability.



As a graphical editor of a media company, this article aims to:

Optimize Financial Performance: Analyze revenue, cost structures, and profitability across ship types and routes to identify key drivers of financial success.
Enhance Operational Efficiency: Examine operational metrics to discover cost-saving opportunities and improve fleet utilization.
Inform Strategic Decision-Making: Leverage data insights to guide investment decisions, route planning, and capacity management for sustainable growth.

Installing and loading packages
The following R packages will be used:

tidyverse: A collection of R packages designed for data manipulation, exploration, and visualization, providing a consistent and easy-to-use syntax.
plotly: R package for creating interactive and dynamic data visualizations.
ggrepel: Enhances ggplot2 plots by preventing text labels from overlapping, ensuring clear and readable annotations.
ggthemes: Offers additional themes and color schemes for ggplot2, enabling more visually appealing and customized plots.
patchwork: Facilitates combining multiple ggplot2 plots into a single layout, making it easy to create complex multi-panel visualizations.
ggridges: Creates ridge plots (or joy plots) to visualize the distribution of a continuous variable across multiple categories.
ggdist: Provides tools for visualizing distributions and uncertainty, including interval plots and density plots.

Data Manipulation
This code chunk below uses the mutate() function to create a new column called Profit in the data frame df. It calculates profit by subtracting Operational_Cost_USD from Revenue_per_Voyage_USD for each row. This operation preserves the existing columns while adding the new Profit column.


Show the code
df <- df %>%
  mutate(Profit = Revenue_per_Voyage_USD - Operational_Cost_USD)


The following code chunks prepare monthly aggregated data for each ship type by converting Date into a monthly format, grouping the data by month, and calculating average values for Revenue_per_Voyage_USD, Operational_Cost_USD, and Profit while ignoring missing values. It then converts the month back to a date format for consistent plotting, enabling trend analysis of revenue, cost, and profit over time.
Overall


Show the code
df_monthly <- df %>%
  mutate(Month = format(Date, "%Y-%m")) %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  summarize(Average_Revenue = mean(Revenue_per_Voyage_USD, na.rm = TRUE),
            Average_Cost = mean(Operational_Cost_USD, na.rm = TRUE),
            Average_Profit = mean(Profit, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(Month = as.Date(paste0(Month, "-01")))

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Be Tradewise or Otherwise
text:
The political turbulence in the United States of America has made global trade one of the most closely watched topics in recent years. Their actions and policies greatly affect the world’s economy and individual countries want to know what impact they will have on their own economies. This assignment examines Singapore’s trade data to gain insights on their economic relationships with other nations.



The goal of this assignment is to critically analyze visualizations from Singapore’s trade report and improve them using ggplot2 and other relevant R packages. The makeover should enhance clarity, readability, and interpretability while ensuring that key trade insights are effectively communicated.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Be Tradewise or Otherwise
text:
Installing and loading packages
The following R packages will be used:

tidyverse: A collection of R packages designed for data manipulation, exploration, and visualization, providing a consistent and easy-to-use syntax.
plotly: R package for creating interactive and dynamic data visualizations.
ggthemes: Offers additional themes and color schemes for ggplot2, enabling more visually appealing and customized plots.
knitr: An R package designed for dynamic report generation. It integrates R code with documents to produce well-formatted reports, tables, and visualizations.
scales: Allows customization of axis labels, breaks, and scales in ggplot2, improving plot readability and presentation.
tsibble: Provides a framework for working with time-series data in a tidy format.
lubridate: Helps parse, manipulate, and analyze date/time information.
feasts: Works with tsibble to analyze time-series components (trend, seasonality, residuals).
readxl: An R package for reading Excel files (.xls and .xlsx) into R.


pacman::p_load(readxl, tidyverse, plotly, ggthemes, knitr, scales, tsibble, lubridate, feasts)

  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`, names_to = "Year_Month", values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  mutate(Trade_Value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(Trade_Value))) 




Filter out the relevant data
For the first visualisation, we are specifically concerned about the Total Merchandise Imports (At Current Prices), Total Merchandise Exports (At Current Prices) and the Total Merchandise Trade (Imports + Exports), (At Current Prices) from 2020 to 2024. Therefore, we filter those rows out.


Show the code
commodity_total <- commodity %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% c("Total Merchandise Imports, (At Current Prices)", "Total Merchandise Exports, (At Current Prices)", "Total Merchandise Trade, (At Current Prices)"))




Show the code
commodity_total <- commodity_total %>%
  mutate(Year = year(parse_date_time(Year_Month, orders = "ym"))) %>% 
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2024) %>%
  group_by(Year, `Data Series`) %>%
  summarise(Total_Trade_Value = sum(Trade_Value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
  ungroup()

Reshape and Filter Only for 2024 and Selected Countries
For the second visualisation, we are specifically concerned about the imports, exports and total trade volume with China, Malaysia, United States of America, Taiwan, Europe, Indonesia, Hong Kong, Republic of Korea, Japan, and Thailand in 2024. Therefore, we filter those rows out. We also combine domestic exports and re-exports into just exports with bind_rows().


Show the code
target_countries <- c("China", "Malaysia", "United States", 
                      "Taiwan", "Europe", "Indonesia", "Hong Kong", 
                      "Korea, Rep Of", "Japan", "Thailand")




Show the code
imports <- df2 %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% target_countries) %>%   
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`,               
               names_to = "Date", 
               values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  filter(startsWith(Date, "2024")) %>%
  mutate(Trade_Type = "Imports") 

exports <- df3 %>%
  bind_rows(df4) %>%  
  filter(`Data Series` %in% target_countries) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`, names_to = "Date", values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  filter(startsWith(Date, "2024")) %>%
  mutate(Trade_Type = "Exports") 




Combine both dataframes


Show the code
combined_trade <- bind_rows(imports, exports)




Calculate Total Trade Volume (Imports + Exports) and merge with combined_trade
Since combined_trade contains both Imports and Exports, we need to group them by Country & Date and sum the values.


Show the code
total_trade <- combined_trade %>%
  group_by(`Data Series`, Date) %>%
  summarise(Trade_Value = sum(Trade_Value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(Trade_Type = "Total Trade") 




Show the code
final_trade <- bind_rows(combined_trade, total_trade)




Summarize Trade Value for the Whole Year of 2024


Show the code
annual_trade <- final_trade %>%
  group_by(`Data Series`, Trade_Type) %>%
  summarise(Trade_Value = sum(Trade_Value, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

Reshape the Data Using pivot_longer()

colnames(df1) <- as.character(colnames(df1))

commodity <- df1 %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`, names_to = "Year_Month", values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  mutate(Trade_Value = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(Trade_Value))) 



Filter out the relevant data
For the first visualisation, we are specifically concerned about the Total Merchandise Imports (At Current Prices), Total Merchandise Exports (At Current Prices) and the Total Merchandise Trade (Imports + Exports), (At Current Prices) from 2020 to 2024. Therefore, we filter those rows out.

commodity_total <- commodity %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% c("Total Merchandise Imports, (At Current Prices)", "Total Merchandise Exports, (At Current Prices)", "Total Merchandise Trade, (At Current Prices)"))


commodity_total <- commodity_total %>%
  mutate(Year = year(parse_date_time(Year_Month, orders = "ym"))) %>% 
  filter(Year >= 2020 & Year <= 2024) %>%
  group_by(Year, `Data Series`) %>%
  summarise(Total_Trade_Value = sum(Trade_Value, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% 
  ungroup()

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Year'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.

Time Series Visualisation
For time series visualisation, the same dataset from V2 will be used, except we will be filtering from 2015 to 2024 and keeping the datasets separate (imports, domestic exports, re-exports).

  filter(`Data Series` %in% target_countries) %>%   
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`,               
               names_to = "Date", 
               values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  mutate(Date = ym(Date)) %>%  
  filter(year(Date) >= 2015 & year(Date) <= 2024)

domestic_ex_v4 <- df3 %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% target_countries) %>%   
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`,               
               names_to = "Date", 
               values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  mutate(Date = ym(Date)) %>%  
  filter(year(Date) >= 2015 & year(Date) <= 2024)

re_ex_v4 <- df3 %>%
  filter(`Data Series` %in% target_countries) %>%   
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Data Series`,               
               names_to = "Date", 
               values_to = "Trade_Value") %>%
  mutate(Date = ym(Date)) %>%  
  filter(year(Date) >= 2015 & year(Date) <= 2024)



Time Series Analysis
For Time Series Analysis, we will need to transpose the dataset and convert the tibble dataset to tsibble.

Transpose and Filter

import1 <- as.data.frame(t(df2))
dom_ex1 <- as.data.frame(t(df3))
re_ex1 <- as.data.frame(t(df4))

colnames(import1) <- import1[1, ]
colnames(dom_ex1) <- dom_ex1[1, ]
colnames(re_ex1) <- re_ex1[1, ]

import_tp <- import1[-1, ]
dom_ex_tp <- dom_ex1[-1, ]
re_ex_tp <- re_ex1[-1, ]

import_tp <- import_tp %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "Date") %>%
  mutate(Date = as.character(Date),   
         Date = ym(Date)) %>%         
  filter(year(Date) >= 2015 & year(Date) <= 2024)  

dom_ex_tp <- dom_ex_tp %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "Date") %>%
  mutate(Date = as.character(Date), 
         Date = ym(Date)) %>%
  filter(year(Date) >= 2015 & year(Date) <= 2024)

re_ex_tp <- re_ex_tp %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "Date") %>%
  mutate(Date = as.character(Date), 
         Date = ym(Date)) %>%
  filter(year(Date) >= 2015 & year(Date) <= 2024)



Convert to tsibble

import_tsibble <- import_tp %>%
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(Date)) %>%
  as_tsibble(index = `Month`)

dom_ex_tsibble <- dom_ex_tp %>%
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(Date)) %>%
  as_tsibble(index = `Month`)

re_ex_tsibble <- re_ex_tp %>%
  mutate(Month = yearmonth(Date)) %>%
  as_tsibble(index = `Month`)



Convert to long format

import_longer <- import_tsibble %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(target_countries),  
               names_to = "Country",
               values_to = "Trade_Value")

dom_ex_longer <- dom_ex_tsibble %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(target_countries),  
               names_to = "Country",
               values_to = "Trade_Value")

re_ex_longer <- re_ex_tsibble %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = all_of(target_countries),  
               names_to = "Country",
               values_to = "Trade_Value")

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Be Tradewise or Otherwise
section: Comments on the visual and analytical results
text:
Comments on the visual and analytical results

There was a sharp increase in exports, both domestic exports and re-exports, around 2020 to our ASEAN neighbours (Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand).
There has been an upward trend in imports in the last 5 years, particularly from Taiwan, the United States and Europe. Exports have been comparatively volatile.
There are several seasonal patterns observed. We see a dip in imports from China, the United States, Hong Kong, Japan and Europe every February with a sharp rise in the following month. Domestic exports are more volatile but we do observe a dip in domestic exports to Taiwan and Republic of Korea every February and a rise in domestic exports to United States. The seasonal pattern for re-exports is similar to that of imports. We see a clear dip in re-exports every February for every region, followed by a sharp rise in the next month. This can be most strongly seen in the data for the Asian countries.
The observed dip in trade volume during February, followed by a rebound in March, is likely due to a combination of factors. The Lunar New Year Effect is the most probable cause, as many businesses in Asia shut down, reducing trade activity in February and recovering in March once operations resume. Additionally, February’s shorter length means fewer working days for trade processing, naturally lowering total trade value compared to other months. Financial cycles may also contribute, as March is the end of the financial year for many businesses in Singapore.

  pivot_wider(names_from=AG, 
              values_from=POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         +rowSums(.[12])) %>%
mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11])+
rowSums(.[13:15]))%>%
mutate(`AGED`=rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
mutate(`TOTAL`=rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%  
mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
/`ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, 
       `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, 
       `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'PA', 'SZ'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.

text:
Box map

ggplot(data = NGA_wp,
       aes(x = "",
           y = wp_nonfunctional)) +
  geom_boxplot()









Creating the boxbreaks function

boxbreaks <- function(v,mult=1.5) {
  qv <- unname(quantile(v))
  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr
  # initialize break points vector
  bb <- vector(mode="numeric",length=7)
  # logic for lower and upper fences
  if (lofence < qv[1]) {  # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {
    bb[2] <- lofence
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
  }
  if (upfence > qv[5]) { # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]
  return(bb)
}



Creating the get.var function

get.var <- function(vname,df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}



Test drive the newly created function

var <- get.var("wp_nonfunctional", NGA_wp) 
boxbreaks(var)

[1] -56.5   0.0  14.0  34.0  61.0 131.5 278.0




Boxmap function

boxmap <- function(vnam, df, 
                   legtitle=NA,
                   mtitle="Box Map",
                   mult=1.5){
  var <- get.var(vnam,df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
     tm_fill(vnam,title=legtitle,
             breaks=bb,
             palette="Blues",
          labels = c("lower outlier", 
                     "< 25%", 
                     "25% - 50%", 
                     "50% - 75%",
                     "> 75%", 
                     "upper outlier"))  +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(main.title = mtitle, 
            title.position = c("left",
                               "top"))
}

title: Hands-on Exercise 8 (Part 1)
text:
Data Wrangling

popdata2020 <- popdata %>%
  filter(Time == 2020) %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from=AG, 
              values_from=POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[3:6])
         +rowSums(.[12])) %>%
mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:11])+
rowSums(.[13:15]))%>%
mutate(`AGED`=rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
mutate(`TOTAL`=rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%  
mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
/`ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, 
       `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, 
       `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'PA', 'SZ'. You can override using the

title: Hands-on Exercise 9
text:
Wrangling attributes

GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(source, target, Weekday) %>%
    summarise(Weight = n()) %>%
  filter(source!=target) %>%
  filter(Weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

the `.groups` argument.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9
text:
Data preparation

GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("sourceLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(from = id) %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("targetLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(to = id) %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(from, to) %>%
    summarise(weight = n()) %>%
  filter(from!=to) %>%
  filter(weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'from'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.
